records.sourceFile: The functional and molecular effects of problematic alcohol consumption on skeletal muscle - A focus on athletic performance.pdf

paper.citation: Caceres-Ayala C, Pautassi RM, Acuña MJ, Cerpa W, Rebolledo DL. The functional and molecular effects of problematic alcohol consumption on skeletal muscle: a focus on athletic performance. Am J Drug Alcohol Abuse. 2022.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of alcohol effects on skeletal muscle in humans, animal models and cell studies, with a focus on sportspeople. Acute and chronic alcohol impair recovery and muscle function through mechanisms that may reduce athletic performance, but binge drinking is understudied.
paper.tldr: Alcohol after hard training can slow muscle recovery and reduce strength and power, especially in men. Most mechanisms come from animal and clinical studies, so staff should treat the performance link as plausible rather than measured in athletes.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed and Google Scholar literature on alcohol and skeletal muscle in humans and animal models, covering acute and chronic exposure, sex differences and molecular mechanisms. The authors summarise human exercise-recovery findings by dose and sex in a single figure.
paper.findings: Acute alcohol after eccentric exercise increased muscle damage and impaired strength recovery in young men at about 1.0 g/kg, but not at 0.5 g/kg or when the exercise was a task participants were trained for; the doses tested in women (0.8 g/kg body mass, 0.88 and 1.09 g/kg lean mass) did not change recovery. Chronic alcohol reduces anabolic signalling and regeneration, and raises inflammation, fibrosis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction in animal and clinical studies.
paper.limitations: Most human studies used a single acute dose in a controlled laboratory, and binge patterns, which are common among athletes, are underrepresented. The review gives no search protocol, and the sport-specific data are small and split by sex.
paper.practicalImplications: Athletes can be told that heavy drinking after hard, unaccustomed eccentric sessions may increase muscle damage and slow strength recovery, particularly in men. The review does not show how repeated binge drinking affects training adaptation, so the acute findings should not be assumed to carry over.
paper.athleteDev: After heavy or muscle-damaging sessions, advise athletes that alcohol at around 1 g/kg may lengthen strength recovery. The review does not give safe intake thresholds for athletes.
paper.rtp: Partly relevant: alcohol after eccentric exercise damage slowed strength recovery in the cited work, but the review includes no injured athletes or return-to-sport tests and cannot set return-to-play timing.
